passage: In their São Paulo flat, Aiko pulled her father's sleeve. "Water, Papa." He filled her cup. When she reached for the stove knob, he said, "No, Aiko. Papa's job." She pulled her hand back and looked at him. Then her friend Valentina's kitten wandered in. Aiko squealed and grabbed its tail. Valentina cried, "Gentle!" Papa showed Aiko how to stroke its back with a flat hand. She copied him, slowly, whispering, "Soft."

qa.q: What did Aiko ask her father for?
qa.a: She asked for water: "Water, Papa."

qa.q: Why did Aiko whisper "Soft" while stroking the kitten?
qa.a: She seemed fond of the kitten and was being careful now, wanting to be gentle after Valentina cried out.

qa.q: How could Papa help Aiko keep being gentle with animals?
qa.a: He can keep showing her the flat-hand stroke and praise her quietly when she uses it. 🙂

qa.q: How does Valentina feel when Aiko grabs the kitten's tail?
qa.a: Valentina is alarmed and protective of the kitten, so cries out "Gentle!"

grounding: Shows a toddler asking for what she needs, accepting a parent's limit, and learning to be gentle with an animal.

passage:
Monday before Diwali: Sharmila held up her picture book, pages facing herself, and asked Deepak across the table, "See the elephant?" Deepak said, "I see the cover!"
Diwali morning: They drew a rangoli peacock on the doorstep. From the other side, Deepak said, "It's upside down." Sharmila walked round to where he stood, stared, and giggled. "It is, from there!"
Two days later: Showing Nani her drawing, Sharmila turned the page round first so it faced Nani.

qa.q: What did the children draw on the doorstep on Diwali morning?
qa.a: They drew a rangoli peacock on the doorstep.

qa.q: What does Sharmila's giggle on Diwali morning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was surprised and amused to find the peacock really did look upside down from Deepak's side.

qa.q: How could Nani help Sharmila keep practising this?
qa.a: She could play games like "What can you see from my chair?" and let Sharmila walk round to check.

qa.q: How does Deepak experience the picture book on Monday?
qa.a: Deepak can only see the cover, so Sharmila's question makes no sense from his seat and he is a little puzzled.

grounding: Illustrates a young child learning, over a festival week, that someone across the way sees a picture differently.

passage: I'm Devika, Akash's didi. It was Makar Sankranti, and Ma had filled the old laddoo tin with kite string. Akash opened it, frowned at the string, and shut it. When Dadu came in, I asked Akash, "What will Dadu think is inside?" He grinned. "Laddoos! But it's string. He'll be wrong." Dadu opened it and groaned. Akash rolled on the floor laughing. Last year he'd have said "string". I don't know exactly what changed in his head, but something did.

qa.q: What had Ma filled the old laddoo tin with?
qa.a: She had filled it with kite string.

qa.q: Why did Akash grin before Dadu opened the tin?
qa.a: He was delighted to know something Dadu didn't, expecting Dadu to think it held laddoos.

qa.q: How could the family keep encouraging this kind of thinking?
qa.a: They could play guessing games about what others know, like asking "What does Ma think is in the box?" before revealing it.

qa.q: What is it like for Dadu to open the tin?
qa.a: Dadu expects a sweet and finds string, so is disappointed for a moment, though the joke brings the family laughing together. 😄

grounding: Shows a young child understanding that his grandfather will wrongly believe a tin holds sweets.

passage: Only ten minutes till the Lohri bonfire, and Gurpreet begged for one more round of hide-and-seek. Aditi counted by the gate. Gurpreet crouched behind the pile of quilts on the cold verandah, then peeked out. "She can't see me," he whispered. When Aditi walked past twice, he pressed a hand over his mouth to keep from giggling. At last he leapt out: "You didn't know!" Aditi laughed. "Next time I'll trick you." Then Mummy called them to the fire.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet hide?
qa.a: He crouched behind the pile of quilts on the cold verandah.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet press a hand over his mouth?
qa.a: He was trying not to giggle, feeling excited and proud that Aditi didn't know where he was.

qa.q: How could the adults keep this kind of playful trick fun and safe?
qa.a: They could mark hiding areas well away from the bonfire and laugh along with both children.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel about being tricked?
qa.a: Aditi takes it in good spirit and even plans a trick back, so the game stays playful for both.

grounding: Illustrates a young child enjoying a playful trick in hide-and-seek and realising the seeker doesn't know where he is.

passage:
Rainy-day note, Aizawl nursery, July
With the playground flooded, Vishal and Lalremsiami spent the morning at the sand tray. They shared the spades and the red bucket and chatted the whole time. Vishal was building "a big road for trucks"; Lalremsiami was making "cakes for my mama's birthday". Each told the other about their project, but neither joined in. When Vishal needed the bucket, he asked and she handed it over. Tomorrow I'll add a second bucket and see if a shared idea grows.
Ms Zohmingthangi

qa.q: What was Vishal building in the sand tray?
qa.a: He was building "a big road for trucks".

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami seem to feel while making her cakes?
qa.a: She seemed happy and absorbed in her own project, content to chat and share without joining Vishal's road.

qa.q: How could Ms Zohmingthangi gently encourage a shared goal?
qa.a: She could suggest a link, like trucks delivering the cakes, and let the children decide whether to join up.

qa.q: What would change if the two had one shared plan?
qa.a: They would need to agree on what they were making, so their chatting would turn into planning and taking turns.

grounding: Shows two young children sharing tools and talking during rainy-season play while each works on a separate idea.

passage: During Ganesh Chaturthi every lane of the Nagpur colony had a pandal, so Omkar and Sangeeta decided to build their own from wooden blocks. "You do the walls, I'll do the roof," Sangeeta said. Omkar lined up the long blocks; Sangeeta balanced flat ones on top. When one wall wobbled, Omkar held it steady while she slid a block behind it. "Now it's strong!" The roof reached Omkar's chin. They set a tiny clay Ganpati inside and ran to fetch Ajji.

qa.q: Who built the walls and who built the roof?
qa.a: Omkar lined up the walls and Sangeeta balanced the roof on top.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she said "Now it's strong!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and relieved that their teamwork had fixed the wobbling wall. 😊

qa.q: What made their teamwork work?
qa.a: They split the jobs clearly and helped each other when a problem came up, like holding the wall steady.

qa.q: What might Ajji think when she sees the pandal?
qa.a: Ajji would likely feel proud and touched that the two children planned and built it together.

grounding: Illustrates young children working together toward one goal, building a festival pandal from blocks.

passage: On a dark December afternoon in Uppsala, Oskar and Astrid played "bakery" under the kitchen table. "I'm the baker and you're the customer," Astrid said. Oskar shook his head. "No, we're both bakers, and Teddy is the customer." Astrid thought, then nodded. "But I make the saffron buns." "Then I make the ginger biscuits." They sold Teddy six pretend buns for three pebbles. When Teddy "forgot" to pay, Oskar made him wash the dishes, and Astrid laughed so hard she bumped her head.

qa.q: How many pretend buns did they sell Teddy?
qa.a: They sold Teddy six pretend buns for three pebbles.

qa.q: What was Astrid thinking when she paused before nodding?
qa.a: She was weighing Oskar's idea and felt happy to share the baker role, as long as she kept the saffron buns.

qa.q: What helped the two keep their pretend game going?
qa.a: Each suggested changes and gave a little, so they built one story they both liked instead of arguing.

qa.q: What would change if Astrid had refused to share the baker role?
qa.a: Oskar might have sulked or walked off, and the shared bakery story could have ended in a quarrel.

grounding: Shows two young children negotiating roles and plot in a shared pretend bakery game.

passage: It was the last week before the winter holidays, and the kindergarten playground was cold and bright. Suraj and Kunal both grabbed the one free swing. "Mine!" "I was first!" Kunal pushed; Suraj fell onto the mat and cried. Ms Rao knelt beside them. "What can we do?" Kunal looked at his shoes. "Sorry I pushed." Suraj wiped his nose. "You go first, then me. Ten pushes each." They counted aloud together, and by the bell they were taking turns pushing each other.

qa.q: How many pushes each did Suraj suggest?
qa.a: Ten pushes each.

qa.q: What does Kunal looking at his shoes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt guilty and embarrassed about pushing Suraj.

qa.q: Why did Ms Rao's question help?
qa.a: Asking "What can we do?" instead of scolding let the boys find their own apology and turn-taking plan.

qa.q: How might Suraj see Kunal after the apology?
qa.a: Suraj seems to forgive Kunal quickly, happy to share the swing and count with him.

grounding: Illustrates young children resolving a fight over a swing with an apology and taking turns.

passage: In April, when autumn leaves covered the park in Cape Town, Tomas and his cousin Zanele filled a shoebox with treasures. At home they tipped it out on the floor. Tomas made piles: "Red here. Yellow here. Brown here." Zanele had a different idea. "Big ones and small ones!" They argued, then Tomas said, "Both!" So they made a big-red pile, a small-red pile, and so on. Zanele found one stone and frowned. "It's not a leaf." She gave it its own pile.

qa.q: Where did the children collect their treasures?
qa.a: They collected them in the park in Cape Town, where autumn leaves covered the ground.

qa.q: Why did Zanele frown at the stone?
qa.a: She was puzzled because it didn't fit any leaf group, and felt it needed its own place.

qa.q: How could an adult build on this sorting game?
qa.a: They could ask the children to sort the same leaves a new way, such as by shape, and explain their groups.

qa.q: How does Tomas feel when Zanele wants to sort a different way?
qa.a: Tomas is annoyed at first, but then finds a way to use both ideas, which keeps the game fun for him too.

grounding: Shows young children sorting autumn leaves by colour and size, and noticing an item that fits neither group.

passage:
"This is my magic wand," said Tanuja, waving a twig she'd found outside the Durga Puja pandal.
"It's just a stick," said her sister Shalini.
"No! It turns you into a frog. Zap!"
Shalini crossed her arms. "I wanted that stick for my flag."
"Frogs can't have flags. Ribbit!"
"Maa, she always takes the best things!"
Maa looked up. "Tanuja, can the wand make flags too?"
Tanuja thought. "Zap! Now it's your flag, Shalini. You're not a frog anymore."
Shalini sniffed, then grinned and waved it.

qa.q: What did Tanuja say her wand does?
qa.a: It turns you into a frog.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: She felt resentful and left out, because she had wanted the stick for her flag.

qa.q: How did Maa's question help the sisters?
qa.a: It invited Tanuja to use her pretend idea to share, so the stick could be a wand and a flag without a fight. 👍

qa.q: What would change if Maa had just taken the stick away?
qa.a: The pretend game would stop, and both girls might end up feeling cross instead of playing together.

grounding: Illustrates a young child turning a twig into a pretend wand, and then into a flag to share with her sister.
